title: Noninteractive SZK versus SZK
formal: Does NISZK equal SZK? Equivalently, does there exist a uniform deterministic polynomial-time reduction that maps every promised pair of sampling circuits X,Y to a sampling circuit Z, preserving the near/far promises specified below?
definitions: A sampling circuit is a finite acyclic Boolean circuit with AND and OR gates of fan-in two, NOT gates, constants, a specified list of random input bits and an ordered list of output bits. Its description explicitly lists gates and wires in binary. Fresh independent uniform bits are supplied to all random inputs; the output distribution is the resulting distribution on bit strings. X and Y may have different numbers of random inputs but have the same output length. For finite distributions P,Q on the same set, \(d_{\mathrm{TV}}(P,Q)=\tfrac12\sum_z|P(z)-Q(z)|\). The source convention for Statistical Difference has YES instances with \(d_{\mathrm{TV}}(X,Y)<1/3\) and NO instances with \(d_{\mathrm{TV}}(X,Y)>2/3\). Inputs between these promises impose no correctness obligation. The reduction outputs one circuit Z with \(m\ge 3\) output bits. On every YES input require \(d_{\mathrm{TV}}(Z,U_{m})<1/m\); on every NO input require \(d_{\mathrm{TV}}(Z,U_{m})>1- 1/m\), where \(U_{m}\) is uniform on \(\{0,1\}^{m}\). The reduction runs in a fixed polynomial of the combined encoded input length on every syntactically valid input, including inputs outside the promise; writing Z and all its input/output nodes counts in that time. It receives no advice or sampling oracle. These are the source’s Statistical Difference and Statistical Difference from Uniform promise problems. Their completeness under deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions makes existence of this reduction equivalent to the original class equality. Thus the complete-problem formulation fixes the question without having to choose a new auxiliary-input or setup convention for protocols.

context_blocks.text: Statistical zero knowledge asks whether a verifier can be convinced while learning only information that a simulator could reproduce. The unresolved equality asks whether interaction adds power when a noninteractive protocol has an honestly sampled public random string.

The same question can be stated entirely in terms of finite sampling circuits. Statistical Difference is complete for SZK, while Statistical Difference from Uniform is complete for NISZK. The requested reduction therefore tests the original class equality with a fully discrete input and output contract.

why: Determine the intrinsic role of interaction in information-theoretic zero-knowledge proofs.
answer_criterion: Provide a Lean proof of a deterministic uniform polynomial-time many-one reduction satisfying both stated promises, or a Lean proof that such a reduction does not exist. The source’s complete-problem equivalence identifies these alternatives with equality or inequality of NISZK and SZK. Randomized reductions or computational zero knowledge concern different targets.

sentences: Statistical zero knowledge studies proofs whose verifier learns no statistically distinguishable information beyond the assertion being proved.
The question is whether every such interactive proof can be replaced by a noninteractive proof with public randomness.
The primary source expresses the same issue as a reduction between two promise problems on sampling circuits.
The reduction must transform close or far pairs into distributions respectively close to or far from uniform.
A deterministic polynomial-time reduction with the specified promises would establish NISZK equals SZK.
